records.current_summary:
Moldova is workable for trans visitors — the best-protected in its immediate neighbourhood. Since 2022, anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes are criminal offences covering SOGI explicitly, and the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover sexual orientation and gender identity; the capital Chisinau's Pride marches through the city centre under police protection, and police have deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters seeking to disrupt it.

Counterweights for a visitor: no accessible legal gender recognition exists for anyone (a medicalised process exists on paper but is reported not functional in practice); the predominant Orthodox Church and major politicians (including the capital's mayor) regularly issue homophobic statements that colour the climate; and the breakaway separatist region of Transnistria, controlled by the neighbouring power Russia, has its own anti-LGBT "propaganda" law — travelers should treat that region as a separate, much riskier jurisdiction.

prison_adds.title: Trăind de gardă/ Deținut transgender – dublu condamnat în închisoare de către „oamenii cu epoleți”
prison_adds.summary: Moldovan investigative outlet Ziarul de Gardă (15 June 2024) documents the four-year detention of Igor Brumarețchi, a transgender man (registered female at birth in 1972, documents changed to male in 2007), who served his sentence in Moldova's penitentiary system, mostly at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca. He says he was held alone in unsanitary, rat-infested cells — including for long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit ('izolator disciplinar') — supposedly for his own safety, while his request for sector 12 (the unit for detainees requiring protection) was refused. He describes staff humiliation: forced strip body searches, 'go to the gynaecologist' calls over the intercom, opening his bathroom door, and calling him 'Natașa' at roll-call, and says only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The National Penitentiary Administration (ANP) replied that he was detained alone 'at his own written request' and without any rights being violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed; Brumarețchi says he will sue in Moldovan courts and the ECtHR, and ZdG has notified the Ombudsman and GENDERDOC-M. Outcome: de facto placement of a trans detainee by birth sex in the men's system with prolonged solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, and no special-unit option.

prison_adds.title: Deținuți ai prejudecăților în instituțiile de stat. Persoane LGBT+, la un pas de suicid. Povestea tragică a unui locuitor al satului Dubna
prison_adds.summary: Observatorul de Nord (7 April 2025) corroborates the same case: Igor Brumarețchi from Dubna village (Soroca district) spent three years locked alone in a cell at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, fully isolated from other detainees and humiliated by prison staff on grounds of sexual orientation, which brought him to the edge of suicide. The piece states the authorities admit homophobia still persists in state institutions and say they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment; the full investigation appeared on anticoruptie.md. Confirms the solitary-style isolation placement practice for a trans detainee in Moldovan prison No. 6 as of 2025.

records.current_summary:
Luxembourg is exceptionally safe — among the strongest trans jurisdictions in its region. Legal gender recognition by self-determination has existed since 2018 (Act of 10 August 2018) with no medical requirements, and notably the process is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is banned across employment, goods, services, education, and health; a national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018; an equality body handles complaints.

No traveler-facing concerns exist: no bathroom laws, no border issues (entry under the common border-free travel zone), no documented anti-trans violence pattern. Gaps are minor: no nonbinary marker, and gender expression and sex characteristics are not explicitly covered in anti-discrimination law — a visitor-specific impact is not documented.

prison_adds.title: Prisons luxembourgeoises : Les détenus gays et transgenres sont protégés
prison_adds.summary: L'essentiel (26 August 2015), reporting Justice Minister Félix Braz's parliamentary answer to LSAP MP Cécile Hemmen, documents that Luxembourg prisons place inmates who disclose or openly show LGBT/trans identity so they are sheltered from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners, with trans-detainee situations handled case by case (the administration gathers all available information on the prisoner); such cases are described as 'exceptional'. Requests by LGBT detainees to be placed in an ordinary section are generally granted, and the minister warned against solutions that would stigmatise or isolate these detainees. A 1989 grand-ducal regulation requires staff to address detainees by surname, and penitentiary staff honour a detainee's chosen 'Monsieur'/'Madame' form of address. The Justice Ministry kept no statistics on LGBT prisoners (disclosure cannot be compelled without illegal privacy interference), and the planned Uerschterhaff prison (Sanem) was designed with multiple sections so detainees could be separated by sex, personality, grounds of detention and, among these, sexual orientation. Outcome: placement follows disclosed identity/need on a case-by-case basis with no codified birth-sex rule and no documented special custody unit or solitary/administrative-segregation practice for trans prisoners in Luxembourg.

records.current_summary:
Honduras is dangerous for trans visitors. It is the site of the hemisphere's defining transfemicide case: Vicky Hernández, a trans woman and activist shot dead in 2009, whose case reached the regional Inter-American Court of Human Rights — which in 2021 found the Honduran state itself responsible for her death and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime. The ruling ordered reforms (including legal gender recognition, which Honduras has partially implemented), but violence against LGBT people remains at levels Amnesty called “epidemic,” driving mass asylum-seeking.

Nothing criminalises being trans, and the Vicky Hernández ruling created formal obligations; a name-change process exists. But gangs, security forces, and social actors all contribute to a documented pattern of violence against trans women in particular, and prosecution remains rare.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, but outing-violence probability is among the highest in the region, outside the two largest countries.

prison_adds.title: Penitenciarias Nacionales de Honduras: una tortura para personas LGTBI - Corresponsales Clave
prison_adds.summary: Corresponsales Clave (trans activist Kendra Jordany, 6 Sep 2017), drawing on the torture-prevention centre CPTRT: trans women in Honduras' national penitentiaries are held in the MEN'S system. At Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara, LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the 'La Isla' module (located beside the mentally-ill unit); trans women are forced to cut their hair and barred from presenting as women ('la policia... dicen que ellas son hombres'); conjugal visits are denied. At Penitenciaria de Marcala authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after CPTRT intervention was she isolated from the men and her feminine belongings returned. Documents birth-sex placement with de facto LGBTI grouping and ad-hoc protective isolation, and no placement-by-gender-identity policy.

prison_adds.title: HRW, 'Every Day I Live in Fear': Violence and Discrimination Against LGBT People in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, and Obstacles to Asylum in the United States
prison_adds.summary: Human Rights Watch (7 Oct 2020), Honduras section: 'Honduras places transgender women in men's prisons, which can lead to physical and sexual abuse.' A Honduran judge told HRW of a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards; the judge said she had informed prosecutors, who did not investigate: 'There's no way to protect trans women in men's prisons.' Independent confirmation that placement operates by birth sex in the men's system, with documented sexual violence and official inaction (as of 2020).

records.current_summary:
El Salvador demands real caution from trans visitors — in an unusual transition. Historically it was among the world's most dangerous places for trans women (documented life expectancy of 35 years, among the lowest anywhere; the Camila Díaz Córdova case — a trans woman deported from the US and killed — became the first hate-crime homicide prosecution of its kind). Since 2022, President Bukele's gang crackdown collapsed the national homicide rate by ~98% (107 to 1.9 per 100k), dramatically reducing the gang violence that drove much anti-trans predation.

The trade-off is a state of exception (an exceptional security regime) with mass arbitrary detention (tens of thousands imprisoned, over 75,000 reported, minimal due process) — a risk mechanism that falls on anyone police decide to target, including gender-nonconforming people, with no effective recourse. There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative name change only), no SOGI hate-crime statute, and no institutional protection infrastructure.

prison_adds.title: Jennifer, la mujer trans que sobrevivio a las torturas en las carceles del regimen de excepcion (GatoEncerrado)
prison_adds.summary: GatoEncerrado (Oscar Hernandez, 26 Feb 2024): since the state of exception began (Mar 2022), trans women arbitrarily captured in mass raids are held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. Jennifer, arrested 14 Apr 2022 in San Salvador, was held first at the 'El Penalito' police lockups and then in prison, where custodians forcibly shaved her hair ('para que sepan lo que son'), singled her out with another trans woman (Rosa) for outdoor punishment drills (handcuffed, forced squatting in the sun), and denied her HIV clinic access; a judge freed her after ~4 months finding the arrest unsupported, while Rosa remains imprisoned. Organisations (Socorro Juridico Humanista, Cristosal) link the abuse to the absence of a Gender Identity Law. Documents birth-sex placement in the general prison system with trans-targeted abuse and no special custody provision.

records.current_summary: Turkey presents real, structured danger for trans visitors — institutionalised, presidential-level hostility that has become state policy. Police profile and detain trans women for identity checks (20 detained in Istanbul in July 2025), trans women have historically been frequent targets of torture and ill-treatment by police, and a trans woman attacked with a knife was herself detained (victim-criminalised). Transphobic attacks and Pride-event violence are documented, and foreign visitors must carry original passports at all times — creating outing risk at the frequent transit checkpoints. A draft law leaked in October 2025 would criminalise LGBT people — not yet passed but under active government consideration. The risk is concentrated in urban trans-visible contexts (Istanbul's Beyoğlu/Tarlabaşı) rather than package-holiday tourist zones, but the institutional hostility pervades.

prison_adds.title: Rights groups urge probe into 'suspicious' death of transgender prisoner in Turkey (Stockholm Center for Freedom)
prison_adds.summary: SCF (18 Dec 2025): transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and Turkish rights groups (coordinated from Human Rights Association / IHD branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakir, Mersin and Aydin) demanded an independent investigation and changes to 'detention practices affecting transgender prisoners'. Kaos GL-cited accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers say four transgender inmates were collectively sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators only entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; opposition MP Sevda Karaca (EMEP) raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025. The case documents that Turkey holds trans prisoners in gendered facilities by registered sex (a trans man was held in a women's prison) and that trans-prisoner custody conditions were formally contested at the state level in late 2025.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQI+ prisoners are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches (Kaos GL), reporting the Prison Insider 'Country Profile' on Turkey (with CİSST data)
prison_adds.summary: Kaos GL (7 May 2024), covering the Prison Insider Country Profile report on Turkey prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association (CISST) and using ILGA World data: LGBTI+ prisoners in Turkish prisons are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches and to de facto isolation, being placed in solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and sometimes refusing to go to hospital out of fear of other male prisoners during transfers. CISST observations quoted in the article state that there is no policy or staff training to identify and address LGBTI+ prisoners' needs, that Turkish prison administration is built on a binary, heteronormative system, that LGBTI+ prisoners are frequently transferred (disrupting visits and solidarity), and that complaints are ineffective and can lead to further violence. The piece documents that Turkey manages trans and LGBTI+ prisoners through segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement.
